title: Fast contextualization: reading notes & scratchpad
body:
Quick context: tossing my scattered notes from papers and light experiments about making long-context interactions cheaper and more robust. Mostly: techniques for fast contextualization (prefix reuse, sparse retrieval within KV cache, chunked attention), tradeoffs, and ideas I want to try on the local bench before proposing anything for runtime. Notes are messy —

Summary takeaways (high level):
- "Fast Contextualization" style approaches (paper A, arXiv 2601.x) emphasize partial KV reuse + light-weight index to avoid re-encoding huge prefixes every request. Good for multi-turn dialogs and retrieval-augmented generation where prefix evolves slowly.
- Sparse key-indexing (LSH or PQ) to find reusable KV slices reduces memory and compute but introduces staleness and retrieval noise — need robust fallback.
- Chunked or sliding attention windows + stale-KV heuristics deliver most latency wins when typical golden prefix length >> effective attention horizon.

Notes to self / insights: 
- Re-encoding the whole conversation each request is dominant cost for short/medium responses; shaving that with cached KV pieces seems high ROI.
- The runtime-team's existing KV cache exposes an API but retrieval is linear scan; that's fine for small pools but will not scale for Dedicated pools with many concurrent sessions. Consider adding a tiny index per sequence group.
- Quantization of KV tensors (8->4-bit experiments) gave mixed results in the toy bench: throughput +18% but BLEU/LLM-quality proxies dropped ~0.6% on some prompts. Need targeted evals.

Papers skimmed (quick bullets):
- "Efficient KV Reuse for Long Contexts" (arXiv:2601.01234) — key idea: hierarchical KV shards + probabilistic caching. Pros: clear SLO-friendly fallbacks; cons: complex eviction heuristics.
- "Sparse Retrieval over KV Memory" (ICML workshop short) — uses PQ index on key vectors; retrieval recall matters more than exact L2 distance for downstream generation.
- "Chunked Attention with Soft Stitching" — shows chunk boundary artifacts can be smoothed with overlap + small cross-chunk attention; small latency penalty for large quality win.

Practical experiments to run (local VM / small GPU):
1) Microbench: baseline nctx=4096 full re-encode vs partial cached KV reuse (toy convs). Metrics: per-request latency (p50/p95), tokens/sec, extra mem.
   - Hypothesis: for avg pref len 2k, partial reuse reduces p95 by ~30% on my 8g GPU.
2) Indexing: implement a simple L2 tree (faiss IVF-lite) on top of the runtime KV cache and compare retrieval latency vs linear scan for 10k keys.
3) Quantized-KV: try 4-bit asymmetric quantization on KV store and evaluate on small eval set of 200 prompts.

Quick design notes for a potential runtime PR: 
- Add lightweight index abstraction to KV cache with two implementations: linear (current) and approximate (IVF/PQ). Keep retrieval timeout that falls back to linear if index fails.
- Expose per-session cache hints: "pinned keys" (never evict), "temporal decay" (score keys by last_hit_time).
- Telemetry: per-hit cost, miss rate, stale-hit rate (when reused kv produces generation regression).

Open questions / risks: 
- How do we measure "staleness" robustly? Need automated A/B eval harness that compares outputs when using cache vs fresh encode on a representative prompt corpus. Hard to do cheaply.
- Interaction with model quantization: do quantized KV reads amplify generation errors? Initial toy results say yes in some cases.
- Multi-tenant Dedicated pools: memory isolation + index overhead could increase tail latencies if not sharded smartly.

To-dos (short):
- [ ] Draft a small RFC for adding index abstraction to runtime KV cache (outline + perf targets).
- [ ] Implement microbench #1 and push results to the PR branch. Link: runtime/pull/482 (forked).
- [ ] Build a 200-prompt eval set from chat logs (PII filtered) to test staleness and quality regressions.

Ideas for evals (cheap proxies):
- LM logprob delta between fresh encode vs cached encode on same seed — use as proxy for quality drift.
- BLEU/ROUGE on synthetic tasks (QA with exact answers) to detect hallucination regressions.
- Prompt-sensitivity score: measure rank-order of next-token logits — large shifts indicate potential quality issues.

Random scribbles / inspiration: 
- Maybe combine a short-term raw KV cache (fast, lossy quant) + long-term exact index for cold retrievals. Use tiered eviction.
- Could piggyback on routing policies: route uncertain cache hits to a mixed-mode handler that does a cheap verification pass (partial re-encode of last N tokens) before generating.

Links worth saving:
- arXiv paper above and references inside it.
- small faiss/ivf tutorial for quick prototyping.
- internal slack convo: #kv-cache-design (see linked artifact).

Notes to self for writing up: keep the RFC small and concrete — perf numbers, clear fallback flows, and one canary rollout plan. Need to ask SRE about memory accounting for per-session indices.

End of notes — these are messy; will clean up into a short RFC after I have microbench numbers.

Questions for Leah (collab):
- Do we have existing telemetry that ties generation quality regressions to cache usage? If not, should instrument logprob deltas as a starting metric?

-- Michael
